children: New Zealand's top central banker said on Thursday that a gradual removal of monetary stimulus was appropriate to return inflation to within the bank's target range, although core inflation may rise in the near term due to the indirect effects of higher fuel prices.

"We do expect (core inflation) to continue increasing somewhat over the coming months," Reserve Bank of New Zealand Governor Anna Breman told a parliamentary committee after the release of the central bank's rate decision on Wednesday.

New Zealand's central bank lifted the cash rate by 25 basis points to 2.75% on Wednesday and signalled more tightening ahead, but stressed any further moves would be measured as it warned of mounting risks to the economic outlook.

Breman said that the forward-looking official cash rate track showed the probability of another rate hike. "But we also said that now after having done two OCR increases we can probably take some time to assess and see how this has affected the economy and whether we see stronger or less strong second-round effects from the high fuel prices."

The central bank sees signs that the economy is recovering. Breman said there were indications that export-led growth is spreading to parts of the economy and while the recovery has been uneven to date, the central bank expects a fuller rebound.

Breman also said youth unemployment was high in New Zealand, which was a concern. She said the committee had discussed whether this was due to firms investing in new technologies and it getting more difficult to enter the labour market. "This is a really difficult question. There's a difference between... what monetary policy can do and not do in this space," she said. "Actually, we see quite a few structural changes in the economy right now and we find them important."
